name: Desmond Whitlock
presenting_complaint: Generalised weakness and palpitations; potassium 7.1 mmol/L flagged on bloods

conditions: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
medical_history.social: Lives with wife. Ex-smoker. Reduced oral intake and diarrhoea over 3 days.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 71-year-old man with CKD stage 4 presents with generalised weakness and palpitations. Venous bloods flag potassium 7.1 mmol/L. He is bradycardic at 52 bpm. He takes perindopril, spironolactone and was started on trimethoprim 3 days ago for a UTI. Obs: BP 146/88, HR 52, RR 18, SpO2 97% RA, GCS 15.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Symptom history: weakness, palpitations, paraesthesia; assess for oliguria/anuria and fluid intake
Medication review for potassium-raising drugs: ACE inhibitor (perindopril), potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone), trimethoprim, NSAIDs, potassium supplements
Screen for causes: AKI-on-CKD, dehydration/diarrhoea, rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, acidosis, Addison's; ask about missed dialysis if relevant
Baseline renal function/eGFR, usual potassium, and allergy documentation
objective: 12-lead ECG IMMEDIATELY and place on continuous cardiac monitor — look for peaked T waves, flattened P waves, widened QRS, sine-wave pattern
Repeat/confirm potassium on a formal (non-haemolysed) venous sample while treating — do NOT wait for the repeat before treating a symptomatic/ECG-positive patient
Assess volume status and urine output (catheter if needed); bloods: UEC, VBG (acidosis), calcium, magnesium, CK, glucose
Focused exam for infection source and signs of fluid overload
assessment: Severe hyperkalaemia (K+ 7.1) with ECG changes (bradycardia) — a medical emergency
Likely multifactorial: CKD-4 plus 'triple' potassium load (ACE inhibitor + spironolactone + trimethoprim) with intercurrent AKI from diarrhoea/dehydration
Consider and exclude pseudohyperkalaemia (haemolysed sample) but treat first if ECG changes present
plan: PROTECT the myocardium: calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL IV over 5–10 min (or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL via central/large-bore access), repeat if ECG changes persist — note this is cardioprotective and does NOT lower potassium

SHIFT potassium intracellularly: 10 units short-acting (actrapid) insulin in 50 mL 50% glucose IV over 15–30 min, AND salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised; add sodium bicarbonate only if significantly acidotic

REMOVE potassium from the body: sodium/calcium resonium (or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) enterally; loop diuretic (e.g. frusemide IV) if fluid-overloaded and passing urine; urgent dialysis if refractory or anuric
CEASE all potassium-raising drugs: stop perindopril, spironolactone and trimethoprim; withhold metformin (AKI)
Monitor: repeat potassium at 1–2 hours and monitor BGL post insulin-glucose (hypoglycaemia risk); continue cardiac monitoring throughout
Refer renal/ICU early for dialysis consideration; treat the underlying trigger (rehydrate, treat infection with a non-nephrotoxic, non-potassium-raising agent)

critical_errors: Believing calcium gluconate lowers the potassium — it only stabilises the myocardium; the note MUST document all three limbs: PROTECT (calcium) AND SHIFT (insulin-dextrose/salbutamol) AND REMOVE (resonium/diuretic/dialysis)
Failing to obtain an immediate ECG and cardiac monitoring in a patient with K+ 7.1
Omitting glucose with the insulin, or failing to monitor BGL afterwards (iatrogenic hypoglycaemia), or continuing the offending potassium-raising drugs
must_not_miss: All three limbs of management documented (protect, shift, remove)
Offending drugs (ACE inhibitor, spironolactone, trimethoprim) ceased and dialysis considered if refractory/anuric
